transcript.content: Hello, please have a seat. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, doctor, it’s... it's kind of a long story, but I guess the main thing that brings me in is that ever since I stopped working, I just can’t seem to slow down. You'd think a guy my age would be thrilled to finally kick his feet up, maybe sit in the recliner and watch some baseball, just take it easy after all those years on the job. My wife certainly thought that was the plan. 

But instead, I wake up before the sun, just like I always did, and I am instantly up and moving. I’ll start by fixing a squeaky hinge on the back door, and then I'm out pulling weeds, and then I'm reorganizing the tool bench... just moving from one little job to the next, all day long. It’s honestly like my brain thinks I still have a whole crew waiting on me to hand out the morning assignments, you know? I'll be pacing the garage like I've got a deadline and a foreman breathing down my neck, but it's just me. I'll finish sweeping the driveway and immediately start looking around for a loose shingle or something to paint. I just keep going and going, and I can't seem to just sit still and enjoy being retired.

Well, you know, my wife asked me that exact same thing just the other day when she caught me power-washing the siding at six in the morning. She said, have you always been this wound up? And I really had to stop and think about it, because, sure, being retired makes it a lot more obvious since I don't have a timeclock to punch or a site manager telling me what to do. But honestly? If I really look back, way, way back... yeah, it's always been there. 

I mean, even back in grade school—and we're talking a long time ago now, back in the day—my teachers used to tell my parents the exact same sort of thing. They'd say I was a bright kid, you know, smart enough to understand the lessons, but I was just completely scattered all over the place. I couldn't keep track of a single thing. I was always losing my pencils, dropping my notebooks, just misplacing my stuff left and right. And I couldn't hold a thought in, either. If I knew the answer to a question, I'd just blurt it right out, calling out over everyone else instead of raising my hand and waiting my turn. It drove the teachers absolutely crazy. They were constantly having to come over and hover over my desk, giving me these reminders to actually sit down and finish my work before the recess bell rang, because otherwise I'd just be off in my own world or trying to talk to the kid next to me. 

So, I guess this motor of mine has been running hot for my whole life, really. It just... it just looks a little different now that I don't have a forty-hour work week to pour all that extra energy into, you know?

Well, it’s funny you should ask about that, because it’s not just the moving around that’s the issue. It’s like my brain is moving just as fast as my feet, maybe even faster. I’ll sit down with a project, right? Let’s say I’m finally going to touch up the paint on the trim around the front windows. I’ve got the brush, I’ve got the little bucket, I’ve got the drop cloth all laid out perfectly. I’m ready to go. I dip the brush in, and then... I don't know, a delivery truck rumbles past on the street. 

Now, a normal person would just think, 'Oh, there goes a truck,' and keep painting. Not me. I hear that truck, and suddenly I’m wondering if it’s the guy bringing that new hose nozzle I ordered last Tuesday. And thinking about the hose nozzle makes me think about the garden, and how I noticed the tomatoes were looking a little wilty yesterday afternoon. And before I even realize what’s happening, the paintbrush is sitting on the drop cloth, the paint is starting to dry on the bristles, and I’m halfway across the yard inspecting the tomato plants, completely forgetting that I was right in the middle of painting the trim. 

Or I’ll sit down to try and write out a little story—I’ve been trying to put down some memories for the grandkids, you know, just little anecdotes from when I was their age. I’ll get a good sentence going, really picturing the old neighborhood, and then I’ll remember that I need to check the oil in the lawnmower. Just like that, the story is gone. Poof. My mind just jumps right over to the garage and the lawnmower, and I completely lose my place on the page. It’s like I can’t keep a fence around my thoughts; they just wander off the second something else catches their eye. It’s exhausting, to be honest with you. You sit down with one intention, and an hour later you’re doing something completely unrelated and you have no idea how you got there.
